contentHtml:
On a two-acre farm outside Bengaluru in southern India, Billy, Jessie and Banu put on their gear, enter a laboratory packed with samples and clock in for a shift detecting early signs of cancer.Their most important diagnostic equipment is their noses.Billy, Jessie and Banu are part of a team of beagles, labradors, Dutch shepherds and other dog breeds being trained by startup Dognosis to sniff out traces of cancer in human breath.

Dognosis is repurposing the canine sense of smell — traditionally used to detect drugs or explosives — for low-cost health screening and aiming to make early detection accessible to far more people.

Advt

Dogs have previously been shown to detect illnesses ranging from cancer to Covid-19, and the two-year-old company aims to apply that capability at scale in India. It joins a small set of start-ups harnessing dogs’ olfactory abilities to develop a non-invasive diagnostic tool with potential uses in public health.

Patients breathe into masks sent to the company’s facility, where dogs are exposed to the sample. Sensors and AI then interpret signals including the animals’ movements, respiration, brain activity and body language to determine whether the sample carries signs of cancer — without imaging scans, blood tests or biopsies.

“It is like finding a needle in a haystack of who in a population has an undiagnosed case of cancer,” said co-founder Akash Kulgod.

Its backers include early stage investors such as Accel India and San Francisco-based Caffeinated Capital among others. They raised $1.5 million via a pre-seed round in 2024 and then an undisclosed sum recently. This is enough for the next two years if the firm sticks to its planned growth trajectory, Kulgod said.The dogs live together at Dognosis’s farm and laboratory, are given walks and playtime and spend 30 minutes to an hour a day on the detection platform, where the work is designed as a game. Their reward: treats.

Advt

During one recent session, two-year-old beagle Whiskey worked through 10 samples, bounding past the first five. At the sixth, she paused, sniffed, moved away and returned, circling for several seconds before the system marked it positive.90% SensitivityIn a Phase 2 study published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, Dognosis reported roughly 90% sensitivity for early-stage cancers across seven broad groups spanning more than 20 cancer types, including breast. According to Kulgod, the dogs also seem capable of expanding their detection abilities: trained on the scent of 10 cancer types, they identified an 11th they hadn’t encountered before.

Advt

The bigger test now is proving that performance holds up outside controlled trials. India has the third-highest prevalence of new cancer cases globally, according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer, while routine screening remains exceedingly rare.The agency estimated 1.5 million new cancer cases and over 900,000 deaths from the disease in India in 2024.Roughly one in 10 Indians are at risk of developing the disease before age 75. Breast cancer was the most commonly diagnosed type, followed by cancers of the lip and oral cavity, lung and cervix.Yet only 1.9% of Indian women surveyed in 2019-2021 said they had ever been screened for cervical cancer, while 0.9% had undergone exams for breast or oral cancer. Among men, just 1.2% reported having undergone oral cancer screening.

Against the backdrop, Dognosis plans to launch an at-home, multi-cancer prescreening test in India next year for a few thousand rupees.Dognosis eventually aims to process 1 million tests a year, double its canine workforce to 30 and halve turnaround times to one week. It is also eyeing the US, where Kulgod said it could open a facility by late 2027 or early 2028.New Jersey startup SpotitEarly has reported similar results from canine cancer-detection trials, though such testing has yet to be commercialized.Getting there will mean showing that accuracy holds across larger, more varied populations, while building the logistics to move and process huge numbers of breath samples. It will also require persuading doctors and patients to trust a screening system built around dogs.Emerging technologies “offer exciting opportunities, but they should strengthen — not replace — existing screening programs,” said Pankaj Chaturvedi, deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Epidemiology at Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai.Dognosis is forging ahead, having kicked off its Phase 3 trial in April with 10 hospitals across India — and plans to recruit about 10,000 people over 12 months. The study will test asymptomatic people at higher risk of cancer and survivors at risk of recurrence, and those flagged will receive conventional follow-up including imaging and biopsy.If the results stand, it plans to launch in Bengaluru next year before expanding across India through partnerships with diagnostic chains and healthcare providers. Kulgod says the test doesn’t need Indian regulatory approval as it’s a prescreening tool, rather than a diagnostic device. Only the latter is regulated in India.“A lot of people recognize we are already depending on dogs in life and death situations,” he said. “The bottleneck all along was: how do you standardize and scale the dog’s nose?”
